# CloudFront and Global Accelerator: say it

<!-- speak:start id=cloudfront-s01 -->
### Prompt 1

**A customer asks.** Does the bucket have to be public for CloudFront to serve our recordings?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** No. The bucket stays private and trusts only your CloudFront distribution. A signed link with an end time decides who can play a recording.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is no. The bucket stays private.

It works like this. The bucket is where your recordings are stored.

The distribution is your CloudFront setup in front of the bucket.

CloudFront sends authenticated requests to the bucket.

The bucket policy allows CloudFront, and only for requests from your distribution.

So a direct link to the bucket fails. Every viewer goes through CloudFront.

And the transfer from the bucket to CloudFront is free.

The thing to watch is this: a private bucket doesn't decide which users can play.

For that, the app gives each signed-in user a signed link with an end time.

After that time, the link stops working.

In your case, a playback link works for a few minutes today.

Should it work longer for very long calls?

**Skeleton.** no, bucket stays private / CloudFront sends authenticated requests / policy allows our distribution only / signed link with end time

**Must say.**

- With origin access control, the bucket policy allows the CloudFront service principal (cloudfront.amazonaws.com) only when the request is on behalf of your distribution.
- Users reach the files through the distribution and cannot access them directly by using Amazon S3 URLs, so no one bypasses CloudFront.
- AWS recommends origin access control (OAC) instead of the older origin access identity (OAI).
- A CloudFront signed URL has an ending date and time, after which the URL is no longer valid.

**Do not say.**

- "we make the bucket public but use random file names". Say: AWS recommends CloudFront in front of the bucket so that it's not publicly accessible. Origin access control keeps the bucket private.
- "an origin access identity is the recommended way to keep the bucket private". Say: AWS recommends origin access control. An origin access identity doesn't work for all scenarios, for example dynamic requests to Amazon S3.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Can we limit a recording link to the computers of one customer office? Yes. When you create a signed URL, you can also set the IP address or range of addresses of the computers that can access the content.
- Does CloudFront also make playback faster for our users abroad? Yes. CloudFront serves content from edge locations closer to the users, so latency is lower. And data transfer from S3 to CloudFront is free.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=cloudfront-s02 -->
### Prompt 2

**A customer asks.** CloudFront or Global Accelerator: which one makes our game faster for players around the world?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Both use AWS edge locations near your players. CloudFront caches downloads such as patches. Global Accelerator carries live TCP or UDP game traffic.

**In 60 seconds.**

Both services meet your players at AWS edge locations near them. The difference is what they carry.

It works like this. CloudFront works with web content over HTTP.

It keeps copies of files, such as patches and images, at the edge.

When a player asks for a cached file, the edge location returns it.

Global Accelerator works with TCP and UDP traffic.

It proxies the packets at the edge to your load balancers or instances in AWS Regions.

Players connect to static IP addresses, and failover between Regions is fast.

The thing to watch is that many games need both services.

CloudFront for downloads, and Global Accelerator for live play.

In your case, patches are large files that many players download.

Does your live game traffic use UDP, and in which Regions does it run?

**Skeleton.** both edge, carry different things / CloudFront: HTTP, cached copies / Global Accelerator: TCP, UDP, static IPs / often both

**Must say.**

- CloudFront improves performance for both cacheable content (such as images and videos) and dynamic content.
- Global Accelerator improves TCP or UDP applications by proxying packets at the edge to applications in AWS Regions.
- Global Accelerator fits non-HTTP use cases such as gaming (UDP), IoT (MQTT), or Voice over IP, and fast regional failover.
- A new accelerator gets two IPv4 static IP addresses.

**Do not say.**

- "Global Accelerator caches your game files at the edge". Say: Global Accelerator proxies TCP or UDP packets at the edge to applications in AWS Regions. CloudFront is the service that returns cached copies.
- "CloudFront can carry our live UDP game traffic". Say: CloudFront supports content sent using the HTTP or WebSocket protocols. UDP traffic is a use case for Global Accelerator.
- "Global Accelerator replaces your load balancers". Say: Global Accelerator sends traffic to endpoints such as Application Load Balancers, Network Load Balancers or EC2 instances. The load balancers stay.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Can our partners allow-list the addresses of the game? Yes. A new accelerator gets two IPv4 static IP addresses from independent network zones. Partners allow-list those addresses, not your instances.
- Do both services help against DDoS attacks? Yes. Both services integrate with AWS Shield for DDoS protection.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=cloudfront-s03 -->
### Prompt 3

**A customer asks.** Every release changes our JavaScript files. Do we invalidate the whole cache each time, or is there a better way?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Put a version in your file names. A new name is a new file everywhere. Keep invalidation for surprises.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: put a version in your file names.

Keep invalidation for the unexpected cases.

It works like this. A new file name is a new object for CloudFront.

It's also new for browsers and company proxies, so they don't return the old copy.

Your HTML page points to the new names after each release.

AWS still recommends an expiration date on the files, even with versions.

The thing to watch is copies outside CloudFront.

Versioning costs less, and a wildcard path counts as one path.

The bigger problem is that invalidation can't reach copies in browsers and proxies.

Users can keep seeing the old version until those copies expire.

In your case, look at your build tool.

Does it already add a hash to your file names?

**Skeleton.** version in file names / new name, new object everywhere / set an expiry anyway / invalidation misses browser copies

**Must say.**

- For frequent updates, AWS recommends that you primarily use file versioning, not invalidation.
- Versioning controls which file a request returns, even when the user has a copy cached locally or behind a corporate caching proxy.
- AWS says to use invalidation only in unexpected circumstances.
- Even if you version your files, AWS still recommends that you set an expiration date.

**Do not say.**

- "invalidation is free". Say: The first 1,000 invalidation paths that you submit each month are free. You pay for each path after that.
- "turn on S3 Versioning to update the files". Say: AWS recommends a version identifier in file names or in folder names. That is a naming practice, not a bucket setting.
- "set every TTL to zero so users always get new files". Say: If Minimum TTL, Maximum TTL and Default TTL are all set to 0, CloudFront caching is disabled.

**Follow-up questions.**

- What if a broken file is already cached and must go now? That is the unexpected case that invalidation is for. A path with the * wildcard counts as one path, and the first 1,000 invalidation paths each month are free.
- How long does CloudFront keep a file if our origin sends no cache headers? Then CloudFront uses the Default TTL of the cache behavior. Its default value is 86400 seconds, which is one day.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=cloudfront-s04 -->
### Prompt 4

**A customer asks.** CloudFront Functions or Lambda@Edge: where should our token check run?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** If the function can check the token from the request alone, use CloudFront Functions. If the check must call your user service, use Lambda@Edge.

**In 60 seconds.**

Both let you run code in CloudFront, close to your users. The difference is what the code can reach.

It works like this. CloudFront Functions are for short, light tasks.

Checking a JSON web token in the request headers is one of them.

They run in under a millisecond, but they have no network access.

Lambda@Edge runs longer, and it can make network calls.

For example, it can call your user service to confirm credentials.

The thing to watch is cost and key data.

CloudFront Functions cost a fraction of the price of Lambda@Edge.

Keep the key data in CloudFront KeyValueStore, so you update it without new code.

In your case, it depends on the token.

Is it a signed JSON web token, or does the check need a database lookup?

**Skeleton.** both run code in CloudFront / Functions: light, no network / Lambda@Edge: network calls, longer / key data in KeyValueStore

**Must say.**

- CloudFront Functions suit request authorization: they can validate authorization tokens, such as JSON web tokens (JWT), by inspecting authorization headers.
- CloudFront Functions have no network access, no file system access and no access to the request body.
- A Lambda@Edge function can make network calls to external resources, for example to confirm user credentials.
- CloudFront Functions run in submillisecond time, and Lambda@Edge functions can run up to 30 seconds.

**Do not say.**

- "CloudFront Functions can call your API to check the token". Say: CloudFront Functions have no network access. A check that calls another service needs Lambda@Edge.
- "CloudFront Functions replace Lambda@Edge". Say: CloudFront Functions is meant to complement Lambda@Edge, not replace it. You can use both on different event triggers within the same cache behavior.
- "Lambda@Edge is always faster". Say: CloudFront Functions run in submillisecond time. Lambda@Edge functions can run up to 30 seconds.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Can we use both in the same distribution? Yes. You can use CloudFront Functions and Lambda@Edge on different event triggers within the same cache behavior.
- How big can a CloudFront function be? The maximum function size is 10 KB, and this quota isn't adjustable. For more data, you create a key value store.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->
